zhou-daguan.name: Zhou Daguan
zhou-daguan.summary: A Chinese diplomat of the Yuan dynasty who visited Angkor in 1296–1297 and wrote a detailed account, a key source for understanding the Khmer Empire.

khmer-empire.name: Khmer Empire
khmer-empire.summary: A Southeast Asian empire centered on Angkor in what is now Cambodia, lasting from 802 to 1431 CE and ruling much of mainland Southeast Asia before likely collapsing due to droughts and floods damaging its water infrastructure.

srivijaya.name: Srivijaya
srivijaya.summary: A Buddhist thalassocratic empire based on Sumatra from the 7th to 11th century that dominated much of maritime Southeast Asia and its trade routes, especially with China.

majapahit.name: Majapahit
majapahit.summary: Javanese Hindu-Buddhist empire based on Java that at its 14th-century peak held sway over much of Southeast Asia, before collapsing in 1527.

nasi-goreng.name: Nasi goreng
nasi-goreng.summary: A Southeast Asian fried rice dish seasoned with sweet soy sauce, shrimp paste and chilli, regarded as a national dish of Indonesia and part of Malaysia's culinary heritage.

angkor-thom.name: Angkor Thom
angkor-thom.summary: The last and most enduring capital city of the Khmer Empire, established in the late 12th century by King Jayavarman VII and covering an area of 9 square kilometres.

ta-prohm.name: Ta Prohm
ta-prohm.summary: A temple near Siem Reap, Cambodia, built largely in the late 12th and early 13th centuries by King Jayavarman VII as a Buddhist monastery dedicated to his mother.

angkor-wat.name: Angkor Wat
angkor-wat.summary: The largest religious complex in the world, built between 1113 and 1150 as a Hindu temple dedicated to Vishnu before gradually becoming a Buddhist site from the late 13th century onward.

banton-romblon.name: Banton, Romblon
banton-romblon.summary: A municipality on Banton Island in the Philippines, inhabited since pre-colonial times and known for producing the Banton cloth, the oldest surviving ikat textile in Southeast Asia.

ikat.name: Ikat
ikat.summary: A resist-dyeing technique from Southeast Asia in which bundles of yarn are bound and dyed before weaving to create patterned cloth, later associated especially with Indonesian textiles.

sukhothai-kingdom.name: Sukhothai Kingdom
sukhothai-kingdom.summary: Siamese kingdom centred on the city of Sukhothai in present-day Thailand, formed in the 13th century and absorbed into Ayutthaya in 1438.

one-pillar-pagoda.name: One Pillar Pagoda
one-pillar-pagoda.summary: Historic Buddhist temple in Hanoi built in 1049 and enlarged by 1105, famous for its single-pillar 'lotus pedestal' structure; one of Vietnam's two most iconic temples.

l-th-i-t-ng.name: Lý Thái Tông
l-th-i-t-ng.summary: Second emperor of the Lý dynasty, ruling Đại Việt from 1028 to 1054, considered the most successful Vietnamese emperor since the 10th century.

chola-dynasty.name: Chola dynasty
chola-dynasty.summary: A Tamil dynasty from southern India that built an expansive maritime empire, reaching its height in the 9th to 13th centuries CE under rulers such as Rajaraja I.

imperial-citadel-of-th-ng-long.name: Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long
imperial-citadel-of-th-ng-long.summary: Complex of historic buildings in central Hanoi, begun in 1010 under the Lý dynasty; largely rebuilt in 1805 and partly demolished by the French.

ba-nh-square.name: Ba Đình Square
ba-nh-square.summary: A square in Hanoi where Ho Chi Minh proclaimed Vietnam's independence on 2 September 1945, and where his mausoleum now stands.

l-dynasty-x.name: Lý dynasty
l-dynasty-x.summary: Vietnamese dynasty ruling from 1009 to 1225, founded by Lý Công Uẩn; it established Vietnam's first university and imperial examinations under rising Confucian influence.

butuan-silver-paleograph.name: Butuan Silver Paleograph
butuan-silver-paleograph.summary: A silver strip with undeciphered inscriptions found in Butuan, Philippines, likely dating from the 12th to 15th centuries.

i-vi-t.name: Đại Việt
i-vi-t.summary: The official name of several Vietnamese monarchies centered on modern Hanoi, first adopted as Đại Cồ Việt in 968 by Emperor Đinh Bộ Lĩnh. It lasted, mostly as Đại Việt, until 1804, when it was renamed Việt Nam.

champa.name: Champa
champa.summary: A collection of Cham polities along the coast of central and southern Vietnam from about the 2nd century CE until 1832, shaped from the 4th century onward by Hinduism.

pagan-kingdom.name: Pagan Kingdom
pagan-kingdom.summary: The first Burmese kingdom to unify the regions of modern Myanmar, ruling the Irrawaddy valley for about 250 years from the 9th century and spreading Theravada Buddhism.

shan-states.name: Shan States
shan-states.summary: A collection of Tai (Shan) principalities called möng, ruled by chiefs titled saopha, that became a dominant political force in Upper Burma from the 13th to 16th centuries.

uriyangkhadai.name: Uriyangkhadai
uriyangkhadai.summary: A Mongol general, son of the strategist Subutai, who led 13th-century campaigns conquering the Song dynasty in China and the first Mongol invasion of Vietnam.

hanoi.name: Thăng Long (Hanoi)
hanoi.summary: The name given to Hanoi when Emperor Lý Thái Tổ founded it as capital of Đại Việt in 1010; the city was later renamed Hanoi in 1831.

m-ngke-khan.name: Möngke Khan
m-ngke-khan.summary: The fourth khagan of the Mongol Empire, ruling 1251–1259, who oversaw conquests of Iraq, Syria and the Dali Kingdom; his death without a successor triggered a civil war that split the empire.

kublai-khan.name: Kublai Khan
kublai-khan.summary: Founder and first emperor of the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty of China (r. 1260–1294), grandson of Genghis Khan, who completed the conquest of the Song by 1279.

quy-nh-n.name: Quy Nhơn
quy-nh-n.summary: A ward in Gia Lai province, Vietnam, once the capital of Gia Lai province, historically built on fishing and agriculture and now shifting toward tourism, services and manufacturing.

battle-of-th-n-i-bay.name: Battle of Thị Nại Bay
battle-of-th-n-i-bay.summary: A February 1283 battle in which Yuan dynasty invaders, though outnumbered, broke through Cham defenses near the Champa capital Vijaya, forcing King Indravarman V to retreat and wage guerrilla warfare.

indravarman-v.name: Indravarman V
indravarman-v.summary: King of Champa from 1257 who refused to personally submit to the Mongol Kublai Khan and led a guerrilla campaign after a Mongol invasion of his kingdom in 1282.

singhasari.name: Singhasari
singhasari.summary: A Javanese Hindu-Buddhist kingdom (1222–1292) that succeeded Kediri as the dominant power in eastern Java before collapsing after a vassal's revolt.

kediri-kingdom.name: Kediri kingdom
kediri-kingdom.summary: A Hindu-Buddhist Javanese kingdom based in East Java from 1042 to 1222, also called Panjalu, known for flourishing classical literature.

vijaya-champa.name: Vijaya
vijaya-champa.summary: Capital of the Kingdom of Champa in what is now Vietnam, serving that role from 938 until conquered by Đại Việt in 1471.

raden-wijaya.name: Raden Wijaya
raden-wijaya.summary: A Javanese prince who founded the Majapahit Empire, ruling Java and much of the Nusantara, after defeating an invading Mongol Yuan fleet; reigned from 1292 until his death in 1309.

tr-n-nh-n-t-ng.name: Trần Nhân Tông
tr-n-nh-n-t-ng.summary: Third emperor of the Trần dynasty, reigning over Đại Việt from 1278 to 1293; credited with the decisive victory over the Mongol Yuan dynasty before retiring to found a school of Vietnamese Buddhism.

lan-na.name: Lan Na
lan-na.summary: A kingdom centered on present-day Northern Thailand from the 13th to 18th centuries, strong enough by the 15th century to fight the Ayutthaya Kingdom on equal terms before becoming a vassal state.

mah-va-sa.name: Mahavamsa
mah-va-sa.summary: Historical chronicle of Sri Lanka, composed as a Pali epic poem in the 5th or 6th century, covering the island's history from its legendary beginnings.

ch-h-n.name: Chữ Hán
ch-h-n.summary: The Chinese characters used to write Literary Chinese and Sino-Vietnamese vocabulary in Vietnam, officially used from the Han dynasty's rule until the early 20th century.

ch-n-m.name: Chữ Nôm
ch-n-m.summary: A complex writing system adapting Chinese characters to write vernacular Vietnamese, used mainly between the 15th and 19th centuries by literati such as Nguyễn Du.

l-c-b-t.name: Lục bát
l-c-b-t.summary: Traditional Vietnamese verse form alternating six- and eight-syllable lines, enjoyed by all social classes and used in most Vietnamese folk poetry.

song-th-t-l-c-b-t.name: Song thất lục bát
song-th-t-l-c-b-t.summary: A Vietnamese poetic form combining a couplet of seven-syllable lines with a six-eight syllable couplet, following complex tonal and rhyme rules.

nguy-n-tr-i.name: Nguyễn Trãi
nguy-n-tr-i.summary: Vietnamese poet, politician and Confucian scholar (1380–1442), principal advisor to Lê Lợi against the Ming dynasty and credited with writing his political proclamations and rebellion appeals.

edict-on-the-transfer-of-the-capital.name: Edict on the Transfer of the Capital
edict-on-the-transfer-of-the-capital.summary: An edict issued in 1010 by Vietnamese emperor Lý Thái Tổ moving the capital of Đại Cồ Việt from Hoa Lư to Đại La.
edict-on-the-transfer-of-the-capital.source_title: Edict on the Transfer of the Capital

i-la.name: Đại La
i-la.summary: An ancient fortified city on the site of present-day Hanoi, built by the Tang governor Gao Pian in 866. In 1010 Lý Công Uẩn made it his capital and renamed it Thăng Long after a yellow dragon was reportedly seen nearby.

nguy-n-quang-h-ng.name: Nguyễn Quang Hồng
nguy-n-quang-h-ng.summary: Vietnamese lexicographer and scholar (1940–2025) at Hanoi's Institute of Hán-Nôm Studies, editor in chief of the standard dictionary of the ancient chữ Nôm script.

l-dynasty.name: Lê dynasty
l-dynasty.summary: The longest-ruling Vietnamese dynasty, governing Đại Việt from 1428 to 1789 (with a break from 1527–1533), founded by Lê Lợi after driving out Ming Chinese forces.

tr-n-dynasty.name: Trần dynasty
tr-n-dynasty.summary: Vietnamese dynasty that ruled Đại Việt from 1225 to 1400, defeating three Mongol invasions and presiding over a golden age of Vietnamese language, arts and culture.

champa-i-vi-t-war-1471.name: Cham–Vietnamese War (1471)
champa-i-vi-t-war-1471.summary: A 1471 military campaign by Emperor Lê Thánh Tông of Đại Việt that sacked the Cham capital Vijaya and is regarded as marking the downfall of the kingdom of Champa.

tr-nh-nguy-n-war.name: Trịnh–Nguyễn War
tr-nh-nguy-n-war.summary: Prolonged 17th- to 18th-century civil war between the Trịnh lords of northern Vietnam and the Nguyễn lords of the south, ending in a long stalemate and a century of peace.

h-nguy-n-tr-ng.name: Hồ Nguyên Trừng
h-nguy-n-tr-ng.summary: Vietnamese scholar, official and engineer (1374–1446), eldest son of Emperor Hồ Quý Ly, who wrote the memoir Nam Ông mộng lục under the pen name Nam Ông.

m-ng-ng.name: Mông đồng
m-ng-ng.summary: A class of near-shore, riverine warship that formed the backbone of medieval Vietnamese naval forces for over a thousand years, first recorded around the year 1000.

l-nh-n-t-ng.name: Lý Nhân Tông
l-nh-n-t-ng.summary: Fourth emperor of the Lý dynasty, ruling Đại Việt from 1072 to 1128, the longest reign of any Vietnamese monarch, and founder of Confucian imperial exams.

l-th-i-t.name: Lý Thái Tổ
l-th-i-t.summary: Founding emperor of the Lý dynasty, ruling from 1009 to 1028, who moved the capital to Thăng Long, beginning Hanoi's history as capital.

anterior-l-dynasty.name: Anterior Lê dynasty
anterior-l-dynasty.summary: A dynasty that ruled Đại Cồ Việt (Vietnam) from 980 to 1009, following the Đinh dynasty and preceding the Lý dynasty, over three emperors' reigns.

l-chi-u-ho-ng.name: Lý Chiêu Hoàng
l-chi-u-ho-ng.summary: Ninth and last sovereign of the Lý dynasty, empress of Đại Việt from 1224 to 1225, and the only empress regnant in Vietnamese history.

tr-n-th-i-t-ng.name: Trần Thái Tông
tr-n-th-i-t-ng.summary: First emperor of the Trần dynasty, reigning over Đại Việt from 1226 to 1258 before spending 19 more years as retired emperor; also known for influential Buddhist scholarship.

jayavarman-vii.name: Jayavarman VII
jayavarman-vii.summary: King of the Khmer Empire (1122–1218), the first Khmer king devoted to Buddhism and widely seen as its most powerful monarch, who built the Bayon and introduced a welfare state.

dvaravati.name: Dvaravati
dvaravati.summary: A network of early polities, or perhaps just a shared Buddhist artistic tradition, in what is now central Thailand, dated roughly the 6th to 11th century CE; historians still debate whether it was ever a single kingdom.

temple-of-literature-hanoi.name: Temple of Literature
temple-of-literature-hanoi.summary: A temple to Confucius in Hanoi, founded in 1070, that hosted Vietnam's first national university from 1076 until 1779.

l-th-nh-t-ng.name: Lý Thánh Tông
l-th-nh-t-ng.summary: Third emperor of Vietnam's Lý dynasty (1023–1072), who built the country's first Temple of Literature in 1072, fought Champa, and claimed imperial status, challenging China's view of the world.

mataram-kingdom.name: Mataram kingdom
mataram-kingdom.summary: A Javanese Hindu-Buddhist kingdom, also called Medang, that flourished from the 8th to 11th centuries and built temples including Borobudur and Prambanan.

airlangga.name: Airlangga
airlangga.summary: The only king of Java's Kingdom of Kahuripan, who in the 11th century rebuilt the realm once ruled by his uncle, becoming one of Java's most notable kings.

anawrahta.name: Anawrahta
anawrahta.summary: Founder of the Pagan Empire (1014–1077) and considered the father of the Burmese nation, who unified the Irrawaddy valley and carried out lasting social, religious and economic reforms.

mon-people.name: Mon people
mon-people.summary: An ethnic group of Lower Myanmar and Thailand, among the earliest peoples in Southeast Asia, credited with spreading Theravada Buddhism across the region.

wang-anshi.name: Wang Anshi
wang-anshi.summary: A Chinese politician, poet and philosopher (1021–1086) of the Song dynasty who served as chancellor and pushed through sweeping, controversial economic and military reforms known as the New Policies.

emperor-shenzong-of-song.name: Emperor Shenzong of Song
emperor-shenzong-of-song.summary: Sixth emperor of China's Song dynasty (1048–1085), known for backing Wang Anshi's New Policies and for actively pursuing territorial expansion and fiscal reform.

l-th-ng-ki-t.name: Lý Thường Kiệt
l-th-ng-ki-t.summary: Vietnamese general and eunuch of the Lý dynasty, 1019 to 1105, who led campaigns against Champa and a preemptive invasion of Song China.

yongzhou.name: Yongzhou
yongzhou.summary: A prefecture-level city in Hunan province, China, on the Xiang River, with a 2,000-year history as one of Hunan's four ancient counties.

rajendra-i.name: Rajendra I
rajendra-i.summary: Chola emperor who reigned from 1014 to 1044, under whom the empire reached its peak, extending rule across the Indian Ocean into Southeast Asia.

zheng-he.name: Zheng He
zheng-he.summary: Chinese admiral and diplomat of the early Ming dynasty (1371–1433/1435) who led seven treasure voyages across the Indian Ocean, boosting China's trade and influence as far as East Africa.

song-dynasty.name: Song dynasty
song-dynasty.summary: Imperial Chinese dynasty that ruled from 960 to 1279, later split into a northern and southern period after losing northern China to the Jurchen Jin dynasty, before its conquest by the Mongols.

ming-dynasty.name: Ming dynasty
ming-dynasty.summary: China's last dynasty ruled by the Han majority, reigning 1368 to 1644 after the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty's fall, founded by the Hongwu Emperor.

theravada.name: Theravada
theravada.summary: Buddhism's oldest surviving school, preserving its teachings in the Pali Canon; as of 2010 it made up 36% of Buddhists worldwide, compared to Mahayana's 53%.

pahang.name: Pahang
pahang.summary: A state of Malaysia occupying the basin of the Pahang River, the largest state in Peninsular Malaysia.

mahayana.name: Mahayana
mahayana.summary: The largest branch of Buddhism, developed in India from around the 1st century BCE, distinguished by its own scriptures and its ideal of the bodhisattva who seeks buddhahood to save all beings.

samudera-pasai-sultanate.name: Samudera Pasai Sultanate
samudera-pasai-sultanate.summary: A Muslim kingdom on the north coast of Sumatra from the 13th to 16th centuries, said to have been founded around 1267 by Merah Silu after his conversion to Islam.

marco-polo.name: Marco Polo
marco-polo.summary: Venetian merchant and explorer (c.1254-1324) who travelled the Silk Road to Mongol-ruled China and wrote an account giving Europeans their first detailed look at Asia.

peureulak-sultanate.name: Peureulak (Perlak)
peureulak-sultanate.summary: The first Muslim state in Southeast Asia, located in what is now Aceh, Indonesia, believed to have converted to Islam as early as the 9th century and noted as a busy port visited by Arab and Persian ships.

phan-rang-th-p-ch-m.name: Phan Rang
phan-rang-th-p-ch-m.summary: A former city in Vietnam and capital of Ninh Thuận Province, with a population of about 208,000 as of 2023.

panduranga-champa.name: Panduranga
panduranga-champa.summary: A Cham principality in south-central Vietnam, the rump state of Champa after its destruction by Vietnam in 1471, lasting until the late 17th century.

chams.name: Cham people
chams.summary: An Austronesian people, the original inhabitants of coastal Vietnam and Cambodia, who founded the Hindu-Buddhist kingdoms of Champa from the 2nd century and became largely Muslim by the 17th century.

al-dimashqi-geographer.name: Al-Dimashqi
al-dimashqi-geographer.summary: Medieval Arab geographer (1256-1327) from Damascus who completed his main work in 1300, describing the peoples and lands of Syria and Southeast Asia.

alids.name: Alids
alids.summary: Descendants of Ali, cousin and son-in-law of the prophet Muhammad, split into Hasanid and Husaynid branches and revered across the Muslim world.

southeast-asian-mancala.name: Congkak
southeast-asian-mancala.summary: A Southeast Asian mancala board game played with cup-shaped holes, known as congkak in Malaysia and by other names in Indonesia, the Philippines and Thailand.

nagarakretagama.name: Nagarakretagama (Deśavarṇana)
nagarakretagama.summary: An Old Javanese poem written in 1365 in praise of the Majapahit king Hayam Wuruk, describing the countryside and regions the empire claimed authority over.

hoklo-people.name: Hoklo (Hokkien) people
hoklo-people.summary: A Han Chinese sub-ethnic group, also called Hokkien people, who speak Hokkien and trace their ancestry to southeastern Fujian, with communities across China, Taiwan and Southeast Asia.

malacca.name: Malacca
malacca.summary: State in Malaysia on the Strait of Malacca whose capital, once seat of the Malacca Sultanate, was conquered by Portugal in 1511, ending its local monarchy.

ayutthaya-kingdom.name: Ayutthaya Kingdom
ayutthaya-kingdom.summary: A Thai kingdom centered on the city of Ayutthaya from 1351 to 1767, a major hub of international trade considered a precursor of modern Thailand.

zhu-fan-zhi.name: Zhu Fan Zhi
zhu-fan-zhi.summary: A 13th-century Song dynasty work by Zhao Rukuo describing foreign countries and traded goods, an important source on Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean.

wang-dayuan.name: Wang Dayuan
wang-dayuan.summary: A 14th-century Chinese traveller, born around 1311, who made two long sea voyages across Southeast Asia, South Asia and Africa, recording his journeys in a 1349 account.
